# What "school children's morality" means and why it matters
<cite id="01599d1b-0">Character education frames morality as the cultivation of values, attitudes, and habits that guide behavior and enable mature moral development; schools are central sites where behavior is shaped and moral reasoning, empathy, and social responsibility are fostered.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-1">Effective programs go beyond moral reasoning to respect children's emotional and values development, building morally and socially competent habits such as honesty, discipline, self-confidence, responsibility, and care for the environment.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-2">Contemporary reviews emphasize integrating character principles into curriculum and school practices, including teacher modeling, character-based lessons, extracurriculars, and community service, with collaboration among teachers, parents, and the broader community.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-3">From a philosophical vantage, education should cultivate moral judgment and practical wisdom, aligning with social–emotional and character development (SECD) that teaches and models personal and civic habits of good judgment and care.</cite>

# Evidence-based levers: Social–emotional learning (SEL) and moral development
<cite id="116a3442-0">Twelve meta-analyses across six continents (mostly randomized and quasi-experimental) converge that tested SEL programs in schools produce consistent, medium-to-large effects on social–emotional competencies, prosocial behavior, reductions in conduct problems and emotional distress, and improved academic engagement and performance across diverse demographics.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-1">A meta-analysis of 22 studies (24,510 students) across elementary and middle school shows SEL improves overall academic achievement (g ≈ 0.08), with larger effects in GPA (g ≈ 0.33), and some moderation by grade and design; quasi-experimental studies showed larger effects than RCTs.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-2">Pathways of widely used SEL curricula like PATHS typically yield larger gains in social–emotional skills than in attitudes, relationships, behavior, and academics, indicating SEL's core output is skill-building with downstream prosocial and academic benefits.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">A large synthesis (213 studies; 270,000+ students) finds SEL improves social–emotional skills, attitudes, classroom behavior, academic performance, and reduces conduct problems and emotional distress; follow-ups show long-lasting benefits across socioeconomic and demographic lines, with benefit–cost ratios around 11:1, though generalizability and teacher outcomes are less studied.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-4">Another meta-analysis (32,742 students) finds a significant overall effect of SEL on emotional and behavioral outcomes (g ≈ 0.31), supporting prior literature on the practical impact of SEL programs.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-4">SEL frameworks map closely to character education principles—self-awareness, self-regulation, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making—clarifying how moral reasoning and prosocial conduct are developed through teachable competencies.</cite>

Implication: Embedding SEL into daily classroom practice (explicit instruction, rehearsal, and modeling) is a high-evidence route to strengthen school children's moral character and related behaviors, with benefits in both noncognitive and cognitive outcomes and demonstrable returns on investment.

# Discipline and relationships: Restorative practices versus punitive approaches
<cite id="97faebfa-0">Momentum has grown globally to replace exclusionary discipline with restorative practices, motivated by evidence of long-term harms of suspension and persistent racial disparities; experimental trials suggest restorative initiatives can reduce exclusionary discipline, though broader climate impacts are mixed and need more rigorous evaluation.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-1">Studies of whole-school restorative approaches report positive impacts on behavior, disciplinary outcomes and disparities, and school climate, with an RCT in Pittsburgh showing a 16% reduction in suspension days (significant across student subgroups) and reductions in disciplinary disparities.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-2">A RAND evaluation of Pittsburgh schools similarly found significant suspension reductions—especially among Black and low-income students—through practices like circles, reflective questions, and proactive statements; studies link restorative practices to improved connectedness, belonging, and social–emotional skills (e.g., empathy, communication, conflict resolution), which support prosocial behavior and academic engagement.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-3">A preregistered cluster RCT found no average differences in student-reported climate after one year, but greater in-school exposure to restorative practices was associated with perceived structure, support, equity, and lower bullying—underscoring that implementation fidelity and dose matter as much as program choice.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-4">Analyses across California districts link restorative justice adoption with enhanced school climate, engagement, and academic performance—especially for Black students—when isolated from funding confounds, reinforcing the value of relationship-centered discipline as a moral-education practice.</cite>

Implication: Shift from punitive to restorative, relationship-first discipline supports moral character by repairing harm, restoring belonging, and teaching accountability; however, effects on broader climate are uneven—implementation quality, dosage, and consistent practice are critical.

# Moral education content and activities aligned to character development
<cite id="01599d1b-1">Curriculum-linked "reinforcing character" programs for early adolescents improve social competence, with evidence that programs tailored to lower social competence yield larger gains; citizenship/civic literacy can reinforce national character traits such as discipline, honesty, self-confidence, responsibility, and environmental care.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-2">Schools can integrate character development through explicit curricula, extracurriculars, and community service, emphasizing teacher roles in modeling and reinforcing moral habits; parental and community involvement is a key enabler.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-3">Character education seeks to teach, practice, and model life habits and skills that make people good—aligning with SECD and positioning schools as core to cultivating virtue, civic responsibility, and the capacity to make morally reflective decisions.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Service-learning and cooperative learning are commonly embedded within SEL programs to build empathy and prosocial attitudes; meta-analytic syntheses show these activities contribute to prosocial behavior and improved attitudes about self/others/school.</cite>

Implication: Combine explicit values/citizenship content with experiential activities (cooperative learning, community service, mock deliberations) and sustained modeling to deepen moral understanding and habits.

# Equity, outcomes, and the role of teacher–student relationships
<cite id="116a3442-0">Across meta-analyses, SEL effects are consistent across gender, ethnicity, race, income, and other demographics, with medium-to-large impacts and longer-term persistence in follow-ups, indicating broad accessibility when programs are well-implemented.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-2">Stronger implementation (dosage, fidelity) correlates with stronger effects in SEL, suggesting that teacher expertise, time, and coaching are pivotal for realizing moral-education benefits.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Teacher socioemotional competence supports relationship-building and protects against burnout; improving teacher SEC is linked to longer retention and better classroom climate, reinforcing the moral-education role of staff development.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-1">Restorative practices reduce disciplinary disparities—e.g., Black students, low-income students, and students with disabilities—improving fairness perceptions and connectedness, which are moral-education foundations.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-2">Restorative circles, reflective questioning, and proactive engagement build belonging and community norms of care, mitigating risk behaviors and supporting pro-social conduct.</cite>

Implication: Moral development is intertwined with equity. Programs that reduce suspensions and improve connectedness disproportionately benefit marginalized students and strengthen school-wide moral climate.

# How to implement in Indian/Tamil Nadu schools: a practical blueprint
- Clarify goals and define "character" locally. <cite id="01599d1b-2">Adopt a definition that integrates moral values, attitudes, and prosocial behavior, and align with state/central civics and values education mandates through a coherent curriculum and school practices.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-1">Prioritize social competence for early adolescents and adapt programs for lower social competence; connect to national goals like discipline, honesty, and civic responsibility.</cite>
- Build adult capacity first. <cite id="116a3442-3">Invest in teacher SEL and restorative practices training; coach classroom teachers to model, explicitly teach, and consistently reinforce moral habits, as implementation quality drives impact.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-3">Use adult modeling and structured routines (e.g., circles, reflective questions) to normalize ethical inquiry and accountability.</cite>
- Co-design curriculum and activities. <cite id="116a3442-0">Select evidence-based SEL curricula with daily integration of self-awareness, self-regulation, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making, delivered via cooperative learning, classroom meetings, and service-learning projects.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-2">Blend character-based lessons with extracurriculars and community service, and embed restorative circles and peer-mediated conflict resolution for schoolwide practice.</cite>
- Engage families and communities. <cite id="01599d1b-2">Form parent–teacher partnerships to reinforce moral habits at home and school; involve community role models in service-learning to connect values to real-world civic life.</cite>
- Monitor and adjust. <cite id="97faebfa-3">Track discipline incidents, student-reported climate and bullying, and perceived structure/support/equity; use routine monitoring to ensure dose and fidelity, addressing variability within and across schools.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Use achievement and socioemotional indicators and conduct cost–benefit checks; SEL's benefit–cost ratio is high, but continuous improvement is needed.</cite>
- Avoid pitfalls. <cite id="97faebfa-0">Guard against overreliance on exclusionary discipline; use restorative practices to reduce suspensions and address root harms, not just behaviors.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-3">Prevent "checklist" implementations by linking practices to student voice, consistent follow-up, and reflective inquiry so that structure and support feel authentic rather than performative.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-1">Balance broad, universal SEL with targeted supports for subgroups where effects may be smaller in small-sample trials; use quasi-experimental enhancements and local adaptations to boost equity.</cite>

# Common questions and how to answer them with evidence
- Will these programs push out academics? <cite id="116a3442-0">No—across multiple meta-analyses, SEL improves academic engagement and performance alongside socioemotional gains.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-1">Effect sizes on academic outcomes are small-to-moderate overall but can be larger in certain subgroups (e.g., GPA) and with stronger implementation.</cite>
- Won't discipline reforms just be "soft" and ineffective? <cite id="97faebfa-1">Whole-school restorative approaches have reduced suspensions and improved climate in RCTs and district-scale studies, especially for high-risk groups; they improve connectedness and prosocial norms, which underpin behavior.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-2">Restorative practices teach accountability and conflict resolution, replacing reactive suspensions with proactive repair and community norms.</cite>
- How do we keep this from being indoctrination? <cite id="01599d1b-3">Character education and SEL emphasize reasoned decision-making, moral deliberation, and practical wisdom, not rote conformity; teaching, practice, and modeling of universal habits (e.g., honesty, respect) within democratic classroom communities support reflective citizenship.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-4">SECD-aligned curricula foreground critical thinking and ethical reasoning, positioning moral education as inquiry rather than imposition.</cite>

# A 90-day action plan (ready, reliable, scalable)
- Month 1: Diagnose and plan. <cite id="97faebfa-3">Collect baseline data on discipline incidents, student voice opportunities, and climate; identify priority classes/grades with higher suspensions or low connectedness.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Select an evidence-based SEL program mapped to state civics/character mandates; secure teacher training and coaching (daily 15–20 minute routines).</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-2">Form a parent–teacher "Character and Community" committee to co-design family reinforcement activities.</cite>
- Month 2–3: Launch adult modeling and classrooms. <cite id="01599d1b-3">Adopt daily circles, reflective questions, proactive check-ins; train teachers to model, explicitly teach, and scaffold moral reasoning in content lessons.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-0">Integrate SEL competencies into core subjects via cooperative learning, reflective writing, and micro-skill drills (listening, perspective-taking, responsible decision-making).</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-2">Train staff in restorative conferencing and proactive "statements" to de-escalate common incidents.</cite>
- Month 3–6: Deepen with service and equity focus. <cite id="01599d1b-2">Launch service-learning projects tied to local civic issues (e.g., sanitation, elder care, education for out-of-school youth), aligning with values of responsibility and care.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-1">Implement schoolwide restorative advisories; target disproportionate discipline patterns and reduce suspensions via early, consistent interventions.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Monitor outcomes monthly; adjust coaching and materials where fidelity is low; target coaching to teachers with higher student need.</cite>
- Months 6–12: Sustain, evaluate, expand. <cite id="116a3442-3">Conduct a mid-year external review; expand to additional schools/grades based on positive cost–benefit and equity impacts.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-3">Evaluate student-reported climate and bullying; use qualitative focus groups to ensure student voice is authentic.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-4">Add advanced modules on moral deliberation and community norms to further develop practical wisdom.</cite>

# Key takeaways for Tamil Nadu and India
<cite id="01599d1b-1">Character education is not ancillary—it is a core school responsibility to build discipline, honesty, self-confidence, responsibility, and environmental care, especially during early adolescence when social competence can be reinforced with targeted programs.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-0">SEL and restorative practices provide rigorous, scalable pathways to improve prosocial behavior, reduce conduct/emotional problems, and raise academic outcomes across diverse student backgrounds.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-1">Evidence shows suspension reductions and improved climate when restorative, relationship-first practices are implemented schoolwide with fidelity.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Returns are high: improved socioemotional skills, academic performance, and benefit–cost ratios make moral-education initiatives economically sensible.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-2">Implementation thrives when teachers, parents, and communities co-create routines, projects, and accountability structures that make moral values tangible in daily life.</cite>

Limitations and next steps: India-specific randomized evaluations of moral-education programs are fewer than global ones; however, cross-regional meta-analyses and large-scale district reforms provide strong guidance transferable to Indian contexts. Future work should include cluster-RCTs in Tamil Nadu on SEL + restorative blends, measurement of moral reasoning and prosocial behavior alongside academic metrics, and impact studies on teacher retention and parent engagement under devolution reforms.

# What "school children's morality" means and why it matters
<cite id="01599d1b-0">Character education frames morality as the cultivation of values, attitudes, and habits that guide behavior and enable mature moral development; schools are central sites where behavior is shaped and moral reasoning, empathy, and social responsibility are fostered.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-1">Effective programs go beyond moral reasoning to respect children's emotional and values development, building morally and socially competent habits such as honesty, discipline, self-confidence, responsibility, and care for the environment.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-2">Contemporary reviews emphasize integrating character principles into curriculum and school practices, including teacher modeling, character-based lessons, extracurriculars, and community service, with collaboration among teachers, parents, and the broader community.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-3">From a philosophical vantage, education should cultivate moral judgment and practical wisdom, aligning with social–emotional and character development (SECD) that teaches and models personal and civic habits of good judgment and care.</cite>

# Evidence-based levers: Social–emotional learning (SEL) and moral development
<cite id="116a3442-0">Twelve meta-analyses across six continents (mostly randomized and quasi-experimental) converge that tested SEL programs in schools produce consistent, medium-to-large effects on social–emotional competencies, prosocial behavior, reductions in conduct problems and emotional distress, and improved academic engagement and performance across diverse demographics.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-1">A meta-analysis of 22 studies (24,510 students) across elementary and middle school shows SEL improves overall academic achievement (g ≈ 0.08), with larger effects in GPA (g ≈ 0.33), and some moderation by grade and design; quasi-experimental studies showed larger effects than RCTs.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-2">Pathways of widely used SEL curricula like PATHS typically yield larger gains in social–emotional skills than in attitudes, relationships, behavior, and academics, indicating SEL's core output is skill-building with downstream prosocial and academic benefits.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">A large synthesis (213 studies; 270,000+ students) finds SEL improves social–emotional skills, attitudes, classroom behavior, academic performance, and reduces conduct problems and emotional distress; follow-ups show long-lasting benefits across socioeconomic and demographic lines, with benefit–cost ratios around 11:1, though generalizability and teacher outcomes are less studied.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-4">Another meta-analysis (32,742 students) finds a significant overall effect of SEL on emotional and behavioral outcomes (g ≈ 0.31), supporting prior literature on the practical impact of SEL programs.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-4">SEL frameworks map closely to character education principles—self-awareness, self-regulation, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making—clarifying how moral reasoning and prosocial conduct are developed through teachable competencies.</cite>

Implication: Embedding SEL into daily classroom practice (explicit instruction, rehearsal, and modeling) is a high-evidence route to strengthen school children's moral character and related behaviors, with benefits in both noncognitive and cognitive outcomes and demonstrable returns on investment.

# Discipline and relationships: Restorative practices versus punitive approaches
<cite id="97faebfa-0">Momentum has grown globally to replace exclusionary discipline with restorative practices, motivated by evidence of long-term harms of suspension and persistent racial disparities; experimental trials suggest restorative initiatives can reduce exclusionary discipline, though broader climate impacts are mixed and need more rigorous evaluation.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-1">Studies of whole-school restorative approaches report positive impacts on behavior, disciplinary outcomes and disparities, and school climate, with an RCT in Pittsburgh showing a 16% reduction in suspension days (significant across student subgroups) and reductions in disciplinary disparities.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-2">A RAND evaluation of Pittsburgh schools similarly found significant suspension reductions—especially among Black and low-income students—through practices like circles, reflective questions, and proactive statements; studies link restorative practices to improved connectedness, belonging, and social–emotional skills (e.g., empathy, communication, conflict resolution), which support prosocial behavior and academic engagement.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-3">A preregistered cluster RCT found no average differences in student-reported climate after one year, but greater in-school exposure to restorative practices was associated with perceived structure, support, equity, and lower bullying—underscoring that implementation fidelity and dose matter as much as program choice.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-4">Analyses across California districts link restorative justice adoption with enhanced school climate, engagement, and academic performance—especially for Black students—when isolated from funding confounds, reinforcing the value of relationship-centered discipline as a moral-education practice.</cite>

Implication: Shift from punitive to restorative, relationship-first discipline supports moral character by repairing harm, restoring belonging, and teaching accountability; however, effects on broader climate are uneven—implementation quality, dosage, and consistent practice are critical.

# Moral education content and activities aligned to character development
<cite id="01599d1b-1">Curriculum-linked "reinforcing character" programs for early adolescents improve social competence, with evidence that programs tailored to lower social competence yield larger gains; citizenship/civic literacy can reinforce national character traits such as discipline, honesty, self-confidence, responsibility, and environmental care.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-2">Schools can integrate character development through explicit curricula, extracurriculars, and community service, emphasizing teacher roles in modeling and reinforcing moral habits; parental and community involvement is a key enabler.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-3">Character education seeks to teach, practice, and model life habits and skills that make people good—aligning with SECD and positioning schools as core to cultivating virtue, civic responsibility, and the capacity to make morally reflective decisions.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Service-learning and cooperative learning are commonly embedded within SEL programs to build empathy and prosocial attitudes; meta-analytic syntheses show these activities contribute to prosocial behavior and improved attitudes about self/others/school.</cite>

Implication: Combine explicit values/citizenship content with experiential activities (cooperative learning, community service, mock deliberations) and sustained modeling to deepen moral understanding and habits.

# Equity, outcomes, and the role of teacher–student relationships
<cite id="116a3442-0">Across meta-analyses, SEL effects are consistent across gender, ethnicity, race, income, and other demographics, with medium-to-large impacts and longer-term persistence in follow-ups, indicating broad accessibility when programs are well-implemented.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-2">Stronger implementation (dosage, fidelity) correlates with stronger effects in SEL, suggesting that teacher expertise, time, and coaching are pivotal for realizing moral-education benefits.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Teacher socioemotional competence supports relationship-building and protects against burnout; improving teacher SEC is linked to longer retention and better classroom climate, reinforcing the moral-education role of staff development.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-1">Restorative practices reduce disciplinary disparities—e.g., Black students, low-income students, and students with disabilities—improving fairness perceptions and connectedness, which are moral-education foundations.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-2">Restorative circles, reflective questioning, and proactive engagement build belonging and community norms of care, mitigating risk behaviors and supporting pro-social conduct.</cite>

Implication: Moral development is intertwined with equity. Programs that reduce suspensions and improve connectedness disproportionately benefit marginalized students and strengthen school-wide moral climate.

- Engage families and communities. <cite id="01599d1b-2">Form parent–teacher partnerships to reinforce moral habits at home and school; involve community role models in service-learning to connect values to real-world civic life.</cite>
- Monitor and adjust. <cite id="97faebfa-3">Track discipline incidents, student-reported climate and bullying, and perceived structure/support/equity; use routine monitoring to ensure dose and fidelity, addressing variability within and across schools.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Use achievement and socioemotional indicators and conduct cost–benefit checks; SEL's benefit–cost ratio is high, but continuous improvement is needed.</cite>
- Avoid pitfalls. <cite id="97faebfa-0">Guard against overreliance on exclusionary discipline; use restorative practices to reduce suspensions and address root harms, not just behaviors.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-3">Prevent "checklist" implementations by linking practices to student voice, consistent follow-up, and reflective inquiry so that structure and support feel authentic rather than performative.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-1">Balance broad, universal SEL with targeted supports for subgroups where effects may be smaller in small-sample trials; use quasi-experimental enhancements and local adaptations to boost equity.</cite>

# Common questions and how to answer them with evidence
- Will these programs push out academics? <cite id="116a3442-0">No—across multiple meta-analyses, SEL improves academic engagement and performance alongside socioemotional gains.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-1">Effect sizes on academic outcomes are small-to-moderate overall but can be larger in certain subgroups (e.g., GPA) and with stronger implementation.</cite>
- Won't discipline reforms just be "soft" and ineffective? <cite id="97faebfa-1">Whole-school restorative approaches have reduced suspensions and improved climate in RCTs and district-scale studies, especially for high-risk groups; they improve connectedness and prosocial norms, which underpin behavior.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-2">Restorative practices teach accountability and conflict resolution, replacing reactive suspensions with proactive repair and community norms.</cite>

# A 90-day action plan (ready, reliable, scalable)
- Month 1: Diagnose and plan. <cite id="97faebfa-3">Collect baseline data on discipline incidents, student voice opportunities, and climate; identify priority classes/grades with higher suspensions or low connectedness.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Select an evidence-based SEL program mapped to state civics/character mandates; secure teacher training and coaching (daily 15–20 minute routines).</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-2">Form a parent–teacher "Character and Community" committee to co-design family reinforcement activities.</cite>
- Month 2–3: Launch adult modeling and classrooms. <cite id="01599d1b-3">Adopt daily circles, reflective questions, proactive check-ins; train teachers to model, explicitly teach, and scaffold moral reasoning in content lessons.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-0">Integrate SEL competencies into core subjects via cooperative learning, reflective writing, and micro-skill drills (listening, perspective-taking, responsible decision-making).</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-2">Train staff in restorative conferencing and proactive "statements" to de-escalate common incidents.</cite>

- Months 6–12: Sustain, evaluate, expand. <cite id="116a3442-3">Conduct a mid-year external review; expand to additional schools/grades based on positive cost–benefit and equity impacts.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-3">Evaluate student-reported climate and bullying; use qualitative focus groups to ensure student voice is authentic.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-4">Add advanced modules on moral deliberation and community norms to further develop practical wisdom.</cite>

# Key takeaways for Tamil Nadu and India
<cite id="01599d1b-1">Character education is not ancillary—it is a core school responsibility to build discipline, honesty, self-confidence, responsibility, and environmental care, especially during early adolescence when social competence can be reinforced with targeted programs.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-0">SEL and restorative practices provide rigorous, scalable pathways to improve prosocial behavior, reduce conduct/emotional problems, and raise academic outcomes across diverse student backgrounds.</cite> <cite id="97faebfa-1">Evidence shows suspension reductions and improved climate when restorative, relationship-first practices are implemented schoolwide with fidelity.</cite> <cite id="116a3442-3">Returns are high: improved socioemotional skills, academic performance, and benefit–cost ratios make moral-education initiatives economically sensible.</cite> <cite id="01599d1b-2">Implementation thrives when teachers, parents, and communities co-create routines, projects, and accountability structures that make moral values tangible in daily life.</cite>

Title: Character Education's Impact On Student Personality: Curriculum And School Practices Review
Snippet: Character encompasses the amalgamation of traits that define an individual, entwining both physical attributes and innate human tendencies that shape interactions with others. Heraclitus, as cited in Ariatama et al., famously proclaimed, "Character is destiny," underscoring the profound impact character exerts on future outcomes. Essentially, one's destiny is intricately woven with the fabric of their character. Building upon this notion, character education emerges as a pivotal step in this interpretative journey, aimed at scrutinizing and comprehending behavior through established societal norms. 1 Character Education's Impact On Student Personality: Curriculum And School Practices Review 53 

Despite its recognized importance, the impact of character education on student personality development has not been sufficiently explored. 2 Previous research has primarily focused on cognitive and academic outcomes, often overlooking the integral role of character education in fostering moral and social competencies. There is a notable gap in understanding how character education is effectively integrated into school curricula and practices, and how it can be optimized to address contemporary challenges faced by students, especially in the context of rapid technological and societal changes. 

This research aims to fill this gap by examining the role of character education in shaping student personality from the dual perspectives of curriculum and school practice. 3 Specifically, it seeks to complement, refine, and challenge existing findings by providing a comprehensive review of both theoretical and practical dimensions of character education. Title: Evidence for Social and Emotional Learning in Schools
Snippet: Each of the 12 meta-analyses empirically synthesized a set of high-quality studies, most of which used methodologically rigorous randomized controlled trials and other controlled comparison group designs that meet the Tier 1 and 2 criteria for evidencebased interventions under the Every Student Succeeds Act. 

Six of the meta-analyses examined programs at all grade levels (PreK-12). Four focused on preschool children. Two focused on secondary school students. The metaanalyses were conducted in Australia, the Netherlands, Romania, the United Kingdom, and the United States and featured studies from around the world. 

In all 12 meta-analyses, effect size was used to measure the impact of SEL programming on various outcomes. Based on hundreds of studies spanning six continents, the findings indicate that there is a consistent, reliable effect of tested, evidence-based SEL programs on students' social, emotional, behavioral, and academic outcomes at all grade levels (PreK-12th grade) and across gender, ethnicity and race, income, and other demographic variables. The effect sizes are classified as medium to large, indicating that the SEL programs studied were substantially beneficial to children. In addition, two of the meta-analyses found that stronger implementation of programs was associated with stronger effects. A summary of the outcomes measured in these meta-analyses and the effects of the SEL programs studied is provided in Table 1. These meta-analyses provide evidence of SEL program effectiveness for students in every grade level (PreK-12) and have shown medium to large effect sizes on the following outcomes: 

• SEL programs, usually taught by classroom teachers, promote the development of social and emotional competencies. 

• Fostering these competencies facilitates positive, prosocial behaviors and positive relationships with others. 

• SEL programs reduce disruptive behavior problems and emotional distress. 

• Fostering these competencies increases students' engagement in learning and subsequently improves students' cognitive and academic performance. 

Longer-term effects were studied in two of these meta-analyses, finding evidence for sustained positive impacts.

Title: The Effect of Social–Emotional Learning Programs on Elementary and Middle School Students’ Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analytic Review
Snippet: This meta-analysis summarized the effects of universal and targeted social and emotional learning (SEL) programs in 22 studies with 24,510 elementary and middle schoolers between 2011 and 2021. It is critical to note that the evidence base was dominated by elementary school research (20 studies), with findings for middle school students derived from only two studies. The current study focused on three main issues: (a) the effectiveness of SEL programs on students’ overall academic performance as well as in specific subjects; (b) possible moderators that could differentiate the overall effectiveness of SEL programs; and (c) possible moderators that presented different effects in different grade levels and subject areas. The results of this review indicated that SEL interventions had a positive effect on overall academic achievement (g = 0.08), elementary school students (g = 0.075), middle school students (g = 0.122), English language arts (g = 0.07), mathematics (g = 0.08), science (g = 0.06), and GPA (g = 0.33) compared to alternative interventions or standard practice. Subgroup analysis was performed with several moderators (i.e., student SES, intervention design, grade level, subject area, and report type). A significant difference was found based on intervention design, with quasi-experimental studies showing larger effect sizes than randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The categorical moderation analysis was performed based on the student’s grade level and subject area and found significant differences. Overall, SEL programs with quasi-experimental designs might be more beneficial for promoting students’ academic performance. Given the limited evidence, conclusions regarding middle school students are preliminary, and more studies on middle school students and students’ science performance are needed.

Title: The effectiveness of Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies program: A meta-analysis
Snippet: The inclusion criteria in the current review were more rigorous than those in previous reviews, especially in terms of research design, sample size and initial equivalence. For instance, more than 20 experimental studies involving PATHS were excluded in the current review since they did not meet our stringent inclusion criteria. These studies were more likely to overestimate the effects since they had small sample sizes or did not have control groups, contributing to the less positive results. Second, the distribution of effects on multiple outcome domains in this review was roughly consistent with the previous ones. Previous reviews showed that the effect sizes of social emotional learning on social emotional skills were substantially larger than those on other outcome domains, including attitude or relations, emotional well-being, prosocial behaviors, conduct problems and academic performance (Durlak et al., 2011;Sklad et al., 2012;Wigelsworth et al., 2016). In this review, the effect size of PATHS on social emotional skills was also higher than those on other aspects. Consequently, the core output of PATHS or other social emotional learning programs was to reinforce students' social emotional skills. Other outcomes, such as promoting prosocial behaviors, reducing problem behaviors, improving academic performance, etc., were all secondary. 

Regarding the methodological factors and implementation features that may moderate the effectiveness, the results of univariate subgroup analysis and meta-regression differed slightly. In the current review, six factors were extracted to explain the heterogeneity of PATHS studies, namely research design, sample size, grade level, social economic status, duration and dosage. Title: Adolescent Exposure to Restorative Practices and Their Perceptions of Support, Structure, and Bullying in the School Climate
Snippet: Momentum for comprehensive school discipline reform has grown with the increasing recognition of the long-term negative effects of school suspension (e.g., Bacher-Hicks et al., 2019) and the persistent racial disparities in exclusionary discipline (Gage et al., 2021). Both internationally and in the United States, schools have turned to restorative practices to reduce the use of exclusionary discipline (e.g., González, 2016). In fact, there is an emerging body of evidence from experimental trials that suggests that restorative practice initiatives can reduce exclusionary discipline (Augustine et al., 2018). Theories of action would indicate that preventionand intervention-oriented restorative practice activities also could improve school climate given that these practices aim to strengthen relationships, repair harm, and increase equity (Evans & Vaandering, 2022). Yet, the few experimental studies addressing the multifaceted theorized outcomes of restorative practices that go beyond school discipline records have provided mixed results (e.g., Acosta et al., 2019;Bonell et al., 2018;Grant et al., 2022; for a review, see Zakszeski & Rutherford, 2021). This study addresses the need for more research by investigating a restorative practice initiative's impact on school climate and the climate of bullying and teasing based on a cluster randomized, controlled trial using student-reported measures after 1 year of implementation. It also examines the degree to which student-reported exposure to restorative practices was associated with positive outcomes across both intervention and control schools. 

This study builds directly on prior findings using data from the same experimental trial of the restorative practice project (Gregory et al., 2022;Huang et al., 2023). In the first study, we showed that students were less likely to be in a discipline incident in the intervention schools than the control schools. The impacts held when accounting for school and student characteristics (students' prior discipline incidents, sex, race, disability status, and income status; Gregory et al., 2022).

Title: Building a Positive School Climate Through Restorative Practices
Snippet: A growing body of research indicates that restorative practices are beneficial. In interpreting this research, it is impor tant to understand that restorative practices are defined in myriad ways across studies. In many cases, studies are focused on narrower approaches to what are often called "restorative justice" programs, which affect relatively few students in a school because they address only interventions for offending be hav ior rather than holistic approaches to improving school climate and relationships. Other studies address the broader range of practices we described earlier that take a schoolwide approach. The evidence for narrow approaches is not as strong as the evidence for universal approaches. For this reason, we have taken great care to clarify what we mean by restorative approaches and to examine studies that seek to utilize a whole school approach. 

As research findings accrue, they point toward positive impacts of restorative approaches on student behavior, disciplinary outcomes and disparities, and school climate. Numerous descriptive studies have found that restorative practices are not only associated with improvement in student be hav ior (e.g., decreases in fighting and bullying), 18 but also with a decrease in office referrals, classroom removals, suspensions, and expulsions. 19 These findings are corroborated by a randomized control trial (RCT) of a whole school restorative initiative, which examines outcomes from the 2015-16 and 2016-17 school years across 44 elementary, middle, and high schools in Pittsburgh, PA. The report finds that program implementation led to a reduction in disciplinary disparities between Black and White students and resulted in a 16% reduction in days lost to suspension, a finding that was statistically significant across several student groups, including Black students, students from low-income families, and students with disabilities. 20 udies also suggest a link between restorative approaches and improved school climate outcomes, including increased levels of student connectedness, improved relationships between students and teachers, and improved perceptions of school climate. 21 For example, an evaluation of a restorative program pi loted in Minneapolis Public Schools found that students were more likely to report that they liked school and had an adult at their schools that they could talk to if they needed help after participating in a restorative conference. 22

Students who reported greater exposure to restorative practices, compared with those reporting less exposure, perceived greater structure, support, and racial/ethnic equality status in their school climate. snippet.text: Despite the popularity of restorative practices in schools, there are only a handful of experimental studies that have examined the effects of restorative practices on student perceptions of school climate, highlighting the need to build the experimental evidence base. Our preregistered cluster randomized, controlled trial examined the impact of the RP Project on school climate. By the spring of the first year of implementation, no intervention effects were found comparing student survey responses in schools randomly assigned to the intervention or control condition. This indicates that restorative practices did not positively (or negatively) change the school climate. We also found that across experimental conditions, students reported a similar frequency in their teachers eliciting their voices and engaging them in repairing harm. The variability in self-reported exposure to restorative practices within schools, however, was associated with student outcomes. Students who reported greater exposure to restorative practices, compared with those reporting less exposure, perceived greater structure, support, and racial/ethnic equality status in their school climate. Further, greater restorative practices exposure was associated with lower perceptions of a climate of bullying and teasing from students and from teachers.

Momentum for comprehensive school discipline reform has grown with the increasing recognition of the long-term negative effects of school suspension (e.g., Bacher-Hicks et al., 2019) and the persistent racial disparities in exclusionary discipline (Gage et al., 2021). Both internationally and in the United States, schools have turned to restorative practices to reduce the use of exclusionary discipline (e.g., González, 2016). In fact, there is an emerging body of evidence from experimental trials that suggests that restorative practice initiatives can reduce exclusionary discipline (Augustine et al., 2018). Theories of action would indicate that preventionand intervention-oriented restorative practice activities also could improve school climate given that these practices aim to strengthen relationships, repair harm, and increase equity (Evans & Vaandering, 2022). Yet, the few experimental studies addressing the multifaceted theorized outcomes of restorative practices that go beyond school discipline records have provided mixed results (e.g., Acosta et al., 2019;Bonell et al., 2018;Grant et al., 2022; for a review, see Zakszeski & Rutherford, 2021). This study addresses the need for more research by investigating a restorative practice initiative's impact on school climate and the climate of bullying and teasing based on a cluster randomized, controlled trial using student-reported measures after 1 year of implementation. It also examines the degree to which student-reported exposure to restorative practices was associated with positive outcomes across both intervention and control schools. 

This study builds directly on prior findings using data from the same experimental trial of the restorative practice project (Gregory et al., 2022;Huang et al., 2023). In the first study, we showed that students were less likely to be in a discipline incident in the intervention schools than the control schools. The impacts held when accounting for school and student characteristics (students' prior discipline incidents, sex, race, disability status, and income status; Gregory et al., 2022).
